claim: The p53 gene is mutated in >50% of cancers.
source: The p53 gene is mutated in >50% of cancers (Kandoth et al., 2013; Hollstein et al., 1991; Petitjean et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Loss of p53 function is considered to be involved in tumor progression, thereby defining TP53 as a tumor suppressor gene.
source: loss of p53 function is considered to be involved in tumor progression, thereby defining TP53 as a tumor suppressor gene (Boutelle and Attardi, 2021; Levine, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The cellular functions mediated by p53 are mainly related to its cellular levels, which increase in response to stress.
source: The cellular functions mediated by p53 are mainly related to its cellular levels, which increase in response to stress, thus activating various mechanisms, for example, cell cycle arrest, cell senescence, cell death, and DNA damage responses (Levine, 2019; Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Lavin and Gueven, 2006; Vogelstein et al., 2000; Hafner et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Cell cycle arrest, cell senescence, and cell death could lead to the removal of damaged cells and could act to suppress tumor formation.
source: Given that cell cycle arrest, cell senescence, and cell death could lead to the removal of the damaged cells, these processes could act to suppress tumor formation (Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Livingstone et al., 1992; Kastan et al., 1991; Clarke et al., 1993; Lowe et al., 1993; Campisi, 2005; Rufini et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: p53 levels are regulated via a mechanism mediated by Mdm2, which constantly degrades p53 by ubiquitination to maintain a low level.
source: p53 levels are regulated via a mechanism mediated by Mdm2, which constantly degrades p53 by ubiquitination to maintain a low level. p53 accumulation occurs when Mdm2 activity is suppressed by stress-induced phosphorylation, which inhibits its ubiquitination activity, resulting in inhibition of p53 degradation (Boutelle and Attardi, 2021; Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Lavin and Gueven, 2006; Haupt et al., 1997; Honda et al., 1997; Kubbutat et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Removing p53 by gene silencing increases the efficiency of induced pluripotent stem cell formation.
source: given that removing p53 by gene silencing increases the efficiency of induced pluripotent stem cell formation (Guo et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Low levels of p53 activity may be required to respond to a broad spectrum of stress through suppression of apoptosis and regulation of metabolisms.
source: it has been suggested that low levels of p53 activity may be required to respond to a broad spectrum of stress (Vousden and Lane, 2007) through suppression of apoptosis and regulation of metabolisms (Boutelle and Attardi, 2021; Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Kruiswijk et al., 2015; Lassus et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: MNNG acts as a DNA-damaging agent by generating methylated bases.
source: the alkylating agent, N-methyl -N′-nitroso-N-nitrosoguanidine (MNNG), which acts as a DNA-damaging agent by generating methylated bases (Wood, 1996; Jacobs and Schär, 2012; Lindahl, 1990; Satoh and Lindahl, 1992; Lindahl et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: O6-methylguanine acts as a premutagenic DNA lesion that induces a G:C to A:T transversion mutation and is repaired by O6-methylguanine methyltransferase.
source: Among MNNG-induced methylated bases, O6-methylguanine, which acts as a premutagenic DNA lesion that induces a G:C to A:T transversion mutation, is repaired by O6-methylguanine methyltransferase

claim: Low levels of p53 in unstressed cells have a role in suppressing the induction of cell death and the formation of aneuploid cells.
source: Those results suggest that the low levels of p53 in unstressed cells indeed have a role in suppressing the induction of cell death and the formation of aneuploid cells

claim: The expansion of Control cells, but not p53 RNAi cells, was suppressed when the damage response was induced, allowing p53 RNAi cells to expand their population compared with the Control cells.

claim: p53 may play a role in both the suppression and the promotion of malignant cell formation during tumorigenesis.
source: These results suggest that, although p53 could suppress the formation of aneuploid cells, which could have a role in tumorigenesis, it could also allow the expansion of cells lacking p53 expression when the damage response is induced. p53 may thus play a role in both the suppression and the promotion of malignant cell formation during tumorigenesis
evidence: Inferred from experimental and simulation results showing dual effects of p53
